rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Change only gradient duration to measure how the crowded early cluster responds to slope. This diagnostic run will distinguish slope-sensitive overlaps from pairs likely to need temperature-dependent selectivity.

Test the high-temperature endpoint against injection 1 to assess selectivity changes in the early three-peak cluster. Higher temperature should also preserve ample room under the 10-minute time threshold.

Retain the favorable 60 C selectivity and make the gradient shallower to improve the remaining R = 1.14 pair. The last peak should still elute before 10 minutes, potentially achieving full resolution without a time penalty.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to change selectivity rather than simply extending the run. Keep temperature and duration fixed to isolate the effect of shifting the gradient window.

Increasing phi0 improved the critical pair from R = 1.14 to 1.32 while preserving the other separations. Test one further grid step to seek full resolution and shorten retention without pushing the first peak into the unretained region.

Injection 6 achieved the maximum CRF; now shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. This tests whether the two closest early pairs retain R ≥ 1.5 under stronger compression.

Lowering phi1 makes the 8-minute gradient slightly shallower, targeting recovery of both marginal early separations. The last peak should remain inside the gradient and elute sooner than in injection 6, which remains the fully resolved fallback.

Test whether another increase in starting organic fraction can shorten the fully resolved method while retaining early-cluster selectivity. Injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method; this run probes the upper useful limit of phi0.

Probe a 5 C temperature decrease at the fastest fully resolved gradient to measure how the two critical early pairs shift relative to each other. This may reveal selectivity headroom for further gradient compression; injection 8 remains the maximum-score fallback.

Return to 60 C and test the intermediate gradient slope between fully resolved injection 8 and slightly under-resolved injection 7. This brackets the fastest fully resolved boundary on the available phi1 grid.

The faster neighboring slopes fall just below full resolution, so test a shallower gradient for a larger resolution margin while retaining the maximum CRF. The last peak should remain comfortably below 10 minutes, and injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Trim the gradient endpoint and duration together, keeping the slope between two fully resolved runs. This should preserve the critical early separations while testing whether a 6-minute programmed gradient is sufficient for the last compound.

Increase the endpoint one grid step to test a slope between injections 8 and 11, bracketing the full-resolution boundary more finely. This could shorten the last-peak time below injection 8 while retaining the maximum CRF, although the critical pair is close to its resolution limit.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores the critical separation at phi0 = 0.20, using injection 9 as the direct comparison. Injection 14 still has a subthreshold pair despite its rounded CRF, so injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

With maximum CRF already secured, probe the opposite temperature endpoint for a different early-cluster elution order that might tolerate a faster gradient. The steep, high-endpoint gradient limits late retention while testing this alternative selectivity regime.

Return to the favorable high-temperature selectivity and test a shallower, trimmed gradient for greater resolution margin. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes while potentially improving robustness over the marginally resolved fastest method.

Test one further reduction in gradient steepness to increase the minimum resolution while aiming to keep the last peak below 10 minutes. The last compound may enter the final hold, so this probes the useful lower endpoint boundary; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Preserve injection 8's gradient slope and early-pair selectivity while reducing the programmed gradient to 4 minutes. This tests whether a final hold at phi1 = 0.50 can elute the later compounds within 10 minutes without sacrificing full resolution.

Refine between injections 8 and 12 to seek a modestly larger resolution margin than the fastest fully resolved method with little added retention time. The low-endpoint hold in injection 19 delayed the last peak, so return to an endpoint that keeps all peaks within the gradient.

Refine the fully resolved high-starting-organic method from injection 15 with a slightly steeper gradient and shorter programmed duration. This should retain its critical separation near R = 1.5 while reducing last-peak time; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether the stronger early-pair separation at higher phi0 and a shallower slope can support full resolution at 55 C. The endpoint should keep late retention manageable, potentially providing a maximum-score alternative below the temperature ceiling.

Make the gradient modestly shallower to lift the remaining R = 1.48 pair above threshold at 55 C. Raising the endpoint simultaneously should keep the last compound within the gradient and likely below the 10-minute penalty boundary.

Refine injection 21 with a slightly steeper, shorter gradient expected to retain full resolution at the higher starting organic fraction. This targets a faster maximum-score alternative, while injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method overall.

Use the final injection to trim injection 12 to a 6-minute gradient while preserving its slope and expected full resolution. The last peak should elute near the gradient end without a time penalty; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed method achieving maximum CRF.
